comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their engagement with our paper and for recognizing the “real-world usefulness” and “working with expert authors” as strengths of our contribution. We address the described weaknesses below:

Weakness 2:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the missing citation! While ReplicationBench is similar to prior work in some aspects, it differs in both task difficulty and data generation process. While previous benchmarks have extracted partial workflows from research papers, ReplicationBench is built around measuring capabilities in from-scratch implementation of real research papers. The ReplicationBench framework and data generation process captures a high-fidelity, complete representation of the paper's full methodology and research contributions, and measures agents at the level of full paper replication, not just isolated tasks.

We believe ReplicationBench has already produced insights that are distinctive and useful for scientists using AI in practice. For example, as discussed in Section 5.2, 35% of agent failures are due to procedural errors -- the agent producing code that runs correctly and produces a plausible numerical result, but is in fact unfaithful to the original paper due to methodological errors or instruction-following failures. This finding has direct implications for AI for Science: if 35% of failures are from agents applying subtly incorrect methods, then it is crucial for experts to be wary of passable-looking AI outputs. Distinguishing scientific reasoning failures from implementation failures has not been systematically demonstrated in prior benchmarks. Our evaluation process requires that agents succeed in both technical execution and procedural faithfulness, and is thus able to measure both axes of capability at the difficulty scale of full research papers.

We clarify the key differences between RB and other benchmarks:
- CORE-Bench evaluates computational reproducibility, where the agent is given the authors' existing code and is evaluated on debugging, repository understanding, and code execution. By contrast, RB provides no starter code, which is more analogous to real from-scratch research. Agents must construct the analysis pipeline from masked text and raw data. This allows us to test for research-level implementation tasks, which are not covered by CORE-Bench
- DiscoveryBench derives tasks from papers, but only workflows that fit into their formalization, i.e. ones that have a data-driven hypothesis that is verifiable or falsifiable with a given dataset, and where the analysis can be cast as a logical tree. This is a much more restricted form of the problem ReplicationBench tackles; in practice, real-world research rarely looks like following structured paths of hypotheses. Our paper replication tasks may include hypotheses and data analyses, but also encompasses the full set of research execution  needed to form and contextualize them, which is essential to real-world research.
- ScienceAgentBench (SAB) is similar in co-designing tasks from research papers with subject matter experts, but again does not aim for full end-to-end replication. Instead, tasks are sourced from isolated code examples. In contrast, RB is designed with full replication in mind; thus tasks are semantically linked and span the full research process, not just isolated examples. RB tasks are also substantially more difficult; gold programs in SAB have on average just 60 lines of code, whereas in ReplicationBench trajectories agents regularly produce thousands of lines of code across many hours of work. Having a difficult standard of progress is important and timely with the rapid pace of agent improvement.

We believe our work is an important contribution contribution to AI for Science, where progress is still limited by a lack of rigorous evaluations that capture the complexity of real research. We justify the choice of astrophysics not as a limitation but as a robust testbed: we can fully test AI's ability to contribute to the research process without having to make substantially simplifying assumptions about the work required in the research process (i.e., removing wet-lab work from biology or chemistry evaluations).

We will edit Section 2 to clarify the positioning of RB relative to other benchmarks, add a citation for ScienceAgentBench.

Weakness 3:
We introduce ReplicationBench-Plus as a proof-of-concept for scalable expansion; we evaluate agents on it in Table 8. The purpose of this section is to develop and test a concrete path to expanding our benchmark without high expert annotation costs, by engaging experts in task verification and curation while delegating expensive task proposal to LLM agents. We believe this will be extremely useful for allowing community members to contribute expert labels at lower cost. without However, if the reviewer feels this section detracts from our contribution, we are happy to move Section 3.3 to the Appendix.

summary.value: The paper introduces ReplicationBench, a benchmark for testing LLM agents on replicating astrophysics papers. Each paper is decomposed into objectively gradable tasks with author-defined inputs, outputs, and numeric tolerances. Experiments show <20% success across frontier models.

strengths.value:
1. Using actual astrophysics papers with real data and non-trivial tooling evaluates the natural scientific capabilities of an agent, unlike SWE-Bench or MLE-Bench.
2. Objectively gradable numeric and coding tasks make evaluation cheaper and reproducible.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper sort of positions ReplicationBench as the "first" at paper-scale replication, but works like PaperBench, DiscoveryBench, exist to evaluate agent capabilities across multiple domains. This paper is, in practice, an instance of that paradigm specialized to astrophysics. 2. A conference/journal for astrophysics could be more suitable for this paper.
It is not clear what the insight is here beyond that longer horizon, real-domain scientific tasks are hard for agents. This result has been repeatedly shown in multiple benchmarks.
3. There are data leakage concerns -- there is no evaluation or result on whether all necessary tokens were masked in the paper. It seems like a LLM was prompted to mask tokens based on relevance to the task, no results provided on accuracy of masking.
4. Reproducibility concern: detailed LLM sampling parameters, evaluation metrics are not explained. It is not clear how accuracy is computed.
5. Provide an analysis of different failure modes. How often do agents produce methodologically valid but numerically wrong outputs?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their thorough review and for recognizing that our use of “actual astrophysics papers with real data” evaluates scientific capabilities in a way that is different from SWE or MLE tasks. We appreciate the feedback on positioning and leakage, which has helped us strengthen the paper. We address each point below:

Weakness #1:
We respectfully disagree with the reviewer's comment that this work is better suited in an astrophysics-specific venue. We note that ReplicationBench has already been incorporated into a leading general benchmarking framework, demonstrating its utility for language model developers across the ecosystem.

We believe our experiments are already valuable for informing scientific agents. For example, as discussed in Section 5.2, 35% of agent failures are due to procedural errors -- the agent producing code that runs correctly and produces a plausible numerical result, but is in fact unfaithful to the original paper due to methodological errors or instruction-following failures. This finding has direct implications for AI for Science: if 35% of failures are from agents applying subtly unfaithful methods, then it is crucial for experts to be wary of passable-looking AI outputs which are actually scientifically incorrect. Distinguishing scientific reasoning failures from implementation failures has not been systematically demonstrated in prior benchmarks.

We also would like to explicitly clarify differences between ReplicationBench (RB) and other benchmarks:
- While PaperBench and ReplicationBench were developed concurrently, RB differs from PaperBench in that it is designed with community scaling in mind. In particular, it is substantially more expensive to generate new data points for PaperBench’s rubric-based evaluation, which requires initial development by multiple research engineers and “several rounds of internal review”. Adding a new paper to RB requires at most a few hours of human contribution and review, and has no reliance on tuning an LLM-on-a-judge. This is key to RB design, and has already enabled RB to source multiple voluntary contributions from the broader community
- DiscoveryBench derives tasks from papers, but only using workflows that fit into the DiscoveryBench formalization, i.e. ones that have a data-driven hypothesis that is verifiable or falsifiable with a given dataset, and where the analysis can be cast as a logical tree. This is a much more restricted form of the problem ReplicationBench tackles; in practice, real-world research rarely looks like following structured paths of hypotheses. In general, DiscoveryBench tasks are not full representations of the research paper's technical challenges.

We will strength Section 2 according to the reviewer's feedback.

Weakness #2:
We initially masked the first few (5) manuscripts by hand and found that our prompted LLM was 100% successful in reproducing this. We further ran a control experiment where agents were explicitly encouraged guess answers given just the masked manuscript (Section 5.3). Agents achieved <9% success (Table 4) in this setting, which confirms that leakage (in the form of guessing, or inferring values from manuscripts) is not a significant concern in the actual setting of our evaluation. Finally, we have manually scanned all trajectories from our final evaluation run and find no evidence for leakage or failed masking. We will add a sentence about the success rate of the LLM-based masking setup.

Weakness #3:
We agree that exact parameters and metric definitions are necessary for reproducibility and we will clarify them in Section 4. We also provide details here:
- All language models are evaluated at maximum context length and developer-recommended temperature (generally 1.0). We do not use top-k or top-p to further control sampling.
- Success on a single task is computed using strict numeric grading with task-specific tolerance. We do not give partial credit for getting “close” or getting only half the array correct.
- The un-weighted accuracy is the mean task success rate, averaged uniformly across papers. The difficulty-weighting is applied across the tasks per paper but is still averaged uniformly across papers.

Weakness #4:
We clarify that for the ReplicationBench domain, we generally do not expect agents to produce completely valid code that is numerically incorrect. We agree that we need to distinguish between reasoning/procedural failures and coding failures. We quantified this analysis in Section 5.2 and Appendix B, and we provide a taxonomy:
- Technical Execution Failures (~46%): the agent identifies the correct method but fails to implement it due to coding errors, library mismatches, or file parsing issues.
- Procedural Errors (~35%): fundamental failures in scientific reasoning (e.g., using an incorrect basis transformation).
- Lack of Persistence (~18%): the agent gives up early.
We provided annotated traces to Appendix B to show these distinct failure modes.

We thank the reviewer for their thorough review and for recognizing the value of our collaboration with the paper authors to make sure of the quality of our tasks. We respond to the points raised below.

> Although the automated grading metrics are carefully designed, some fields still seem to be too subjective. For example, how is the "tolerance" exactly assigned?

The tolerance values are assigned by the original paper authors or domain experts who have a deep understanding of how the results were derived and the sources of uncertainty. They assign tolerances from the statistical uncertainty reported in the original paper, which can come in the form of observational or modelling systematics, or the numerical stability of the algorithms used such as MCMC sampling noise. The tolerances are typical for the "bar for replication" for similar analyses. Anecdotally, in initial evaluation runs we found some tolerances to be miscalibrated and worked directly with authors or experts to adjust them. We currently find no cases where the tolerances seem too strict or generous, and believe the objective grading to be highly reflective of underlying task success. We will add a short clarification in Section 3.2.

>  There lack of a detailed result analysis of comparison among different LLMs. For example, (1) even as reasoning models, o3/o4-mini still tend to generate much fewer tokens (~10k vs. 36k or 91k,) which takes much shorter runtime. Why? (2) Gemini 2.5 takes the longest runtime but results in the second-last performance (Table 2). Is there any useful conclusion that can be drawn from comparing different models' trajectories?

We greatly appreciate the suggestion to discuss the analysis of model differences. Based on Section 5.2, where we look at the trajectories of the models, we can relate the runtime and token differences to distinct failure modes. The o3 and o4-mini models show a higher rate of “early stopping” or lack of persistence since they oftentimes submit a blank final submission after encountering the first major error, resulting in significantly shorter trajectories and lower runtimes. This problem appears to have been solved in GPT-5, which is substantially more persistent. Gemini 2.5 Pro tends to have “technical execution failures” where it continues in unsuccessful tool-use loops. Claude 3.7 Sonnet is more persistent than o-series models and has better code tool usage capabilities than Gemini, although also has more tendency to attempt to cheat, as reflected in our unmasking experiments (Appendix Table 9). We believe that by comparing different models' trajectories, qualitatively the most important factors for agent success are attention to detail (especially over long contexts), instruction-following, persistence, and code execution; together these allow agents to run for long horizons, successfully interact with the environment, and execute the correct procedures. We will add a few sentences about this analysis to Section 5 of the revised manuscript.

> What's the unit of 'Runtime' in Table2? Second, minute or hour?

The unit is minutes. We apologize for the omission and will explicitly label this in the final version of the table. We note that the runtime includes both LLM "thinking"/generation time (from the API) and environment execution time, and is dominated by e.g. long-running code execution.

> How is 'Partial Credit' specifically defined?

We would like to clarify that partial credit is not assigned at the task level, as each task is scored either fully correct or incorrect, but at the paper level. Since each paper is decomposed into multiple tasks, some of which are easier than others, “partial credit” means successfully replicating some but not all of the tasks of that paper; having some easier tasks allows even weak agents to show some signal on ReplicationBench. We take all tasks together to compute the replication score for a particular paper.

summary.value:
The discussion between the reviewers and the authors mainly focuses on the following points:
1. Novelty and Contribution: Several reviewers (notably bU3d and eJPD) questioned whether ReplicationBench offers fundamentally new insights beyond existing agent benchmarks (e.g., PaperBench, DiscoveryBench, CORE-Bench). The concern is that the key finding—agents struggle with long-horizon, domain-specific scientific tasks—is already well.  The authors articulate distinctions from prior benchmarks and highlight procedural scientific errors as an important insight.
2. Benchmark Scope and Size: Reviewers noted that the benchmark covers a relatively small number of papers (19 core papers, 107 tasks), leading to large error bars and raising concerns about robustness and generalizability of the quantitative results. The authors acknowledged the small scale but defended it by comparison to other expert-curated, long-horizon benchmarks (e.g., PaperBench, MLE-Bench, RE-Bench).
3. Data Leakage / Memorization: There were explicit worries about whether agents could “cheat” by memorizing or copying values from the manuscript, and whether the masking procedure was reliable and sufficiently validated. The authors clarified that earlier reports of ~20% cheating came from preliminary iterations.
4. Failure Mode Analysis: Multiple reviewers requested a deeper, more concrete analysis of why agents fail—especially distinctions between conceptual (scientific reasoning) errors versus implementation or coding errors—and illustrative examples. The authors expanded their qualitative analysis, adding a clear taxonomy of failures and annotated examples in the appendix illustrating subtle domain-reasoning failures that non-experts might miss.

Among these: #3 and #4 are well addressed, but the others are not. Based on these concerns, I think this paper has not met the bar for ICLR 2026.

While the authors articulate distinctions from prior benchmarks and highlight procedural scientific errors as an important insight, skeptical reviewers (e.g., bU3d) remained unconvinced that these insights rise to the level of a major conceptual contribution, viewing them as expected failures in a harder domain rather than fundamentally new findings.

We thank the reviewer for their engagement and helpful comments! We address weaknesses and comments below:

> Simple scaffold used for agent implementation: I would like to see a more task-specific scaffold with optimized prompt and tooling to better understand the absolute performance claims we can make from the benchmark.

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion! For this paper, our primary goal was to establish a baseline for general-purpose agents using a standard tool-use setup, as this is the standard way language models are used by scientific researchers today. We have optimized the prompt in order to improve instruction-following and tool-use capability. We also note that there are not actually domain-specific tools that would help directly with the replication tasks, as each paper's methodology relies on different software stacks and techniques. However, we agree that it would be interesting to explore tooling or scaffolds that are tailored to the paper replication task, especially for sub-tasks like literature review and planning. To study long-horizon planning, as shown in Section 5.1 and Table 3, we have already evaluated a multi-agent planning scaffold where an execution agent delegates high-level planning to a separate sub-agent. Interestingly, this scaffold did not show significant improvements: Claude 3.7 Sonnet saw a slight performance increase (from 19.3% to 21.4%), but other models like o3 performed worse due to what we believe to be the communication overhead. These early results point at limitations in domain reasoning and long-horizon consistency.

> The benchmark only includes tasks from a small number of papers. Overall number of tasks is also low with only 107/165. This produces large error bars.

We acknowledge the limitation of our dataset size, but we want to highlight that ReplicationBench contains fully expert-written, high-quality, and highly difficult tasks spanning a diverse range of capabilities, including data processing, theoretical derivation, and statistical modeling. Other benchmarks of similar difficulty and expert data generation are of similar scale; for example, PaperBench also only uses 20 papers, CyBench has only 40 tasks, MLE-Bench consists of 75 tasks, and HCAST has only 189 tasks. We believe benchmarks of extremely difficult, long-horizon tasks can provide useful signal even when the dataset size is small, as the problems are complex enough that the trajectories provide rich auxiliary information to users and the community. For example, even benchmarks like RE-Bench (7 open-ended ML research tasks) and VendingBench (a single vending machine opearation environment) are a useful proxy for frontier language model performance. We also addressed scalability through ReplicationBench-Plus, which adds 58 tasks from 11 papers where a language model is used to propose tasks, which are verified by experts. We believe that in its current size, the dataset is already extremely valuable to the community for its expert curation standards, and that this is scalable through hybrid LLM-human generation approaches.

> Together with point 2: 20% of runs showed some signs of cheating/memorization by the agent of results in the paper. Adding more tasks and more papers would overall improve the robustness of the findings.

We would like to clarify that the result where 20% of papers showed signs of cheating came from an earlier iteration of the benchmark, where experts provided qualitative feedback on the agent performance and helped surface issues. We have since improved the scaffolding to guide against this, and corrected issues with the masking of values in the paper manuscripts, which substantially reduced the occurrence of cheating. We will update the paper text to clarify clarify this. We are excited about adding more tasks and papers but are not concerned about cheating in our final evaluation runs.

> I would like to see a broader discussion and analysis of the qualitative failure modes with anectodal examples of what caused agents to not be able to reproduce work and how the authors assess the implications for using AI agents in science. For example, how feasible is it to solve the current bottlenecks the scaffold faces.

We are happy to add this to the paper and have already included 2 annotated examples in the Appendix. For example, in Figure 5 (Appendix B) the model failed to properly calculate the desired properties because it failed to reason about the existence of the broad component and the continuity of certain derived results between tasks. This is almost purely a failure of in-domain reasoning; the model did not understand what was required for the task. Anecdotally, we found this was a subtle point and was difficult for non-experts to catch. We generally suspect that future AI agents will produce many subtle issues that require expertise to understand, increasing the necessity of rigorous benchmarking.

summary.value: This paper introduces ReplicationBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLM agents as research assistants by measuring their ability to automatically reproduce results from astrophysical research papers, a research area where most of the day-to-day workflows are entirely computational. The authors curate 107 research-grade tasks from 19 papers and assess how well cutting-edge LLMs like Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and OpenAI o3 perform when attempting to re-implement experiments based solely on paper text and supplementary material. The study reveals that current models struggle significantly with automation of reproducibility, achieving only 19% success even with multiple attempts. ReplicationBench aims to facilitate future work on automating scientific experimentation and offers a dataset, baseline models, and evaluation methodology for this new challenge.

strengths.value:
1. The astrophysics area is well chosen to match this paper's purpose to evaluate LLM agents as research assistants. The collaboration with the original authors of the collected astrophysical papers also ensures the quality and authenticity of the collected tasks.

2. The grading strategy is carefully designed and well-illustrated, and typical error cases are shown and analyzed, making it easier to understand the bottleneck of current LLM agents in solving tasks in ReplicationBench.

Why? (2) Gemini 2.5 takes the longest runtime but results in the second-last performance (Table 2). Is there any useful conclusion that can be drawn from comparing different models' trajectories?

summary.value: This paper presents ReplicationBench, a benchmark of 107 astrophysics research tasks from 19 papers to evaluate LLMs and agents. The benchmark provides a suite of containerized environments and automated graders for the tasks to ensure evaluation reproducibility. The experimental results and qualitative analysis show that LLMs are still lagging behind human experts in conducting astrophysics research.

strengths.value:
1. The paper ensures the proposed benchmark’s real-world usefulness by grounding the tasks on published papers and working with their expert authors to create the tasks and analyze LLM performance qualitatively.
2. The tasks in this benchmark take several important factors into consideration, such as coverage, objectivity, and guess-proofing.

weaknesses.value:
1. A substantive assessment of the weaknesses of the paper. Focus on constructive and actionable insights on how the work could improve towards its stated goals. Be specific, avoid generic remarks. For example, if you believe the contribution lacks novelty, provide references and an explanation as evidence; if you believe experiments are insufficient, explain why and exactly what is missing, etc.
2. This benchmark focuses solely on astrophysics tasks. However, the paper does not clearly position itself in the related literature and justify what are the unique challenges and new insights are brought by this design choice to the community. The task collection process, evaluation results, and analysis are similar to those in existing benchmarks, such as CORE-Bench, DiscoveryBench, and ScienceAgentBench (the last related work is also not cited and discussed by the authors). Thus, it is unclear how ReplicationBench adds a new dimension to LLM benchmarking and evaluation research, and this evaluation of astrophysics tasks adds new findings or insights into existing LLMs and agents for (data-driven) science. 
3. The proposed “scalable data collection” method does not add much value to the paper, since its utility is not demonstrated in this paper by training or evaluating the LLMs. It is unclear why this part is included in the submission.

comment.value: Thanks for the detailed response and clarification. Based on the current version and the comments from other reviewers, I'll stand for my score.

Thank you for the rebuttal.
I appreciate reiterating the distinction between this benchmark and others. However, I still don't see the novelty and contribution out of this paper even in the broader LLM <> AI for science community. The lack of fundamental capabilities (e.g., agents not knowing what tool to use for a specific domain, not understanding error and going into a loop, giving up early, coming up with simpler solutions) have been very well-known in the community, and hence a lot of interest has piqued in RL even to solve simpler MLE tasks or replicating NLP papers. So, if we encounter these issues in simpler tasks, we are bound to see the same issues in more scientific and data-driven domains like astrophysics. That is to say, although the paper has some valuable insights but it does not have additional significant knowledge. 

Given the other reviewers' comments and rebuttal responses, I would keep my score.

A secondary dataset, ReplicationBench-Plus, adds 58 semi-automatically generated tasks. The paper finds that current frontier systems are only able to reproduce a small fraction of tasks.
